title: Different generations
caption: The star cluster NGC 1866 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: Ranked #71 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars fill this image from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. They belong to NGC 1866, a star cluster on the outermost fringes of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way. The Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered it in 1826.

NGC 1866 is a surprisingly young globular cluster, and it is close enough for its stars to be studied one by one. Most globular clusters are dominated by old stars with low metallicity; astronomers call any element other than hydrogen and helium a 'metal'. Because stars forge heavier elements over their lives, a star built from unenriched material is taken to be very old, and some globular cluster stars may be among the first to form after the Big Bang.

Here, though, the stars are not all alike. Different generations are thought to live side by side. One idea is that after its first stars formed, the cluster met a giant gas cloud that triggered a fresh wave of star birth, producing a younger population and explaining its youthful look.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using five filters from the U band through visible light to the near-infrared I band. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble separates individual stars in a cluster belonging to another galaxy, something no eye could do, and part of the light it recorded lies beyond what the eye can see.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: How globular clusters form is still debated. Star clusters like this one are bound together by gravity and can contain hundreds of thousands of stars. James Dunlop, who found NGC 1866, went on to list thousands of stars and deep-sky objects over his career.
alt: A field densely filled with the stars of the cluster NGC 1866.
